name: Power Homeschool
line: Power Homeschool teaches video lessons from the start of each course. In AMP, every answer sets the next problem.
description: AMP vs Power Homeschool: Power Homeschool teaches video lessons from the start of each course. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
verdict: Power Homeschool teaches math in courses that start at the beginning. Each lesson is a teacher on video, then practice, and the next lesson opens when the last is done [3][4][9]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test and no test day. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. In Power Homeschool, a student begins each course at the beginning [3]. Its course pages say a student moves quickly through what they already know, and describe Prism Diagnostics, which finds gaps and gives targeted instruction videos [6][7]. Lessons run in order, and the next opens when the last is done [9].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Power Homeschool the unit is the video lesson: a short video taught by a teacher, then practice problems on the concept. If a student does not grasp it, the program offers more in-depth help videos and a Lesson Manual [4]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages. The data are correlational [13].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a learner shows a skill by getting it right without help, more than once, and moves on. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Power Homeschool requires a student to master each concept before the next lesson [4]. We found no statement of what counts as mastery in the pages we read [4][9].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Power Homeschool describes Vectored Instruction, which finds gaps and brings back earlier lesson material to reinforce them [6]. We found no schedule for that review in the pages we read [4][6]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math and runs from counting through precalculus in one program, on one map of skills. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Power Homeschool teaches math in separate grade and subject courses, from kindergarten math through Pre-Calculus, and a student begins each course at the beginning [3][5][6][7].

rows.range: Kindergarten math through Pre-Calculus, in separate grade and subject courses [5][6][7].
rows.start: Each course starts at the beginning [3].
rows.teaching: A short video lesson from a teacher, then practice problems. More in-depth help videos and a Lesson Manual if a concept is not grasped [4].
rows.next: The course's own order: the next lesson opens when the last is done [9]. Prism Diagnostics is described as finding gaps and giving targeted videos [6].
rows.mastery: A student must master each concept before the next lesson [4]. We found no stated rule for what counts as mastery.
rows.review: Vectored Instruction is described as finding gaps and bringing back earlier lesson material [6]. We found no review schedule.
rows.print: Course materials are online [2]. We found no printable workbooks or answer keys.
rows.adult: Supervises and sets weekly goals for each course. The system grades the work [3][9].
rows.reports: Every answer in the Live Monitor, alerts on concepts a student finds hard, course grades, attendance and report cards [9].
rows.evidence: We found no outcome study on its site, no entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [10][11].

theirs: Power Homeschool is run by Power Homeschool LLC. It offers Acellus online courses, from PreK through grade 12, to families who teach at home, and its sign-in links point to Acellus [1][8]. In math it runs from kindergarten through Pre-Calculus, in grade and subject courses, with separate math fact practice courses [5][6][7].

A student begins each course at the beginning [3]. A lesson is a short video taught by a teacher, followed by practice problems on the concept, and the student must master the concept before the next lesson. If a student does not grasp it, the program offers more in-depth help videos and a Lesson Manual [4]. Lessons run in order, and the next opens when the last is done. The parent sets weekly goals for each course and supervises, and the system grades the work [3][9].
credit: A teacher on video for every lesson, with more in-depth help videos when a concept is not grasped [4].
A student must master each concept before moving to the next lesson [4].
The adult can see every problem and answer in the Live Monitor, with alerts on concepts a student finds hard [9].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Power Homeschool on its site. We found no entry for Power Homeschool or Acellus in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [10][11].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [12]. In an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages; the authors estimate the benefit of extra doing at more than six times that of extra watching or reading, and the data are correlational [13]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want a teacher on video to open each lesson, with the course taken in a set order.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no course to begin at lesson one.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want printable workbooks made from your learner's own record, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Power Homeschool?
questions.answer: Power Homeschool teaches math in courses that start at the beginning, each lesson a teacher's video followed by practice [3][4]. AMP has no separate test and no course to start: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Power Homeschool work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Power Homeschool on its site. We found no entry for Power Homeschool or Acellus in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [10][11].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A learner can take other subjects in Power Homeschool and practice math in AMP, which places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
